title: Behçet’s Disease: The Silk Road Vasculitis
summary: An idiopathic, chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder characterized by occlusive vasculitis of both arteries and veins. It is a sight-threatening condition requiring a multidisciplinary approach, most prevalent along the historic Silk Road.

sections.title: Historical Context & Epidemiology
content: Possibly first recognized by Hippocrates.
Modern description: Adamantiades (Greek) and Behçet (Turkish).
Prevalence: Highest along the traditional 'Silk Road' route.
Turkey: Peaking at up to 0.4% of the population.
Demographics: Typically affects young adults (peak onset: third decade).
Geography: Lower prevalence in Europe and North America; high in Middle and Far East.
Mortality: Around 5% at 5–10 years, typically due to cardiovascular or CNS complications.
UK Care: Three National Centres of Excellence (Birmingham, Liverpool, London) established in 2012 for multidisciplinary care.

content.explanation: A transient, mobile hypopyon in a relatively 'white' eye is characteristic of Behçet disease and JIA-associated uveitis. Unlike HLA-B27, the eye is often not as injection-heavy during a hypopyon flare.

branches: Anterior: Acute non-granulomatous AAU, transient mobile hypopyon.
Vitreous: Severe vitritis (universal in active posterior disease), inflammatory deposits on inferior peripheral retina.
Retina: Transient superficial white infiltrates (no scarring), deep retinitis (viral-like), exudative detachments.
Vasculitis: Occlusive periphlebitis & arteritis (contrast to Sarcoid), sheathing, hemorrhages, CMO.
Optic Nerve: Hyperaemia, oedema (secondary to inflammation or raised ICP), atrophy.
End-Stage: Retinal/optic atrophy, attenuated 'ghost' vessels, gliosis, phthisis.

sections.title: Systemic Multi-Organ Involvement
content: Oral: Recurrent aphthous ulceration (scarring or non-scarring).
Genital: GU (Genital Ulceration).
Skin: Erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis, papulopustules, acneiform rash/nodules, Dermatographia.
Joints: Arthritis (mono or poly), though arthralgia is more common.
Vascular: Thromboses (Venous > Arterial), SVC/IVC obstruction, superficial thrombophlebitis, Aneurysms (pulmonary/coronary).
GI: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea (especially ileocecal).
CNS: Meningoencephalitis (brainstem), sinus thrombosis, intracranial hypertension, neuropathies.
Renal/Hepatic: Relatively uncommon.

rows: Recurrent Oral Ulceration (at least 3x in 12 months)
Usually unilateral, very red eye (not white), non-transient hypopyon.
Purely venous involvement (periphlebitis), granulomatous KPs (Behçet is non-granulomatous).
Rapidly progressive necrotizing herpetic retinitis; Behçet retinitis infiltrates may heal without scarring.
The 'Great Mimicker'; requires serology to rule out.
Also presents with hypopyon in a white eye, but usually in children/females with positive ANA.

sections.title: Investigation Workup
content: 1. Clinical Assessment: No specific diagnostic lab test exists.
2. Pathergy Test: Oblique 20g needle insertion; check for sterile pustule at 24–48h (>95% specific).
3. Lab Markers: ESR, CRP, Complement levels, WBC (often elevated).
4. Genetic Testing: HLA-B51 association.
5. Ocular Imaging: FA (delineates ischaemia/leakage), Laser Flare Photometry (correlates with activity).
6. Systemic Imaging: MRI/MRV Brain (Neuro), CT/CTA or MRA for aneurysms/thrombosis.
7. Screenings: Thrombophilia screening, TB screening (prior to biologics).

sections.title: Ophthalmic Complications
content: Cataract & Glaucoma (Steroid-induced or inflammatory)
Neovascularization (NVD/NVE) responding to ischemia
Vitreous Haemorrhage & Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD)
Cystoid Macular Oedema (CMO) and diffuse leakage
Optic Atrophy and Retinal Atrophy (End-stage)
Severe Vision Loss: 2/3 of males at 10 years (historical data)

sections.title: Management Protocols (EULAR/AUS)
sections.content: Liaise with a physician. Referral to National Centres is advised. SYSTEMIC STEROIDS: Initial Prednisolone 1–2mg/kg/d PO; Pulsed IV Methylprednisolone (1g/d for 3d) for acute flares. STEROID-SPARING AGENTS: Azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg daily), Ciclosporin (2–5 mg/kg daily), Mycophenolate Mofetil, Methotrexate, Tacrolimus. BIOLOGICS: Infliximab or Adalimumab (Anti-TNF) considered early for vision-threatening disease. INTERFERON-ALFA: Alternative for severe disease (do not combine with Azathioprine due to myelosuppression). NOTE: Topical steroids alone are rarely adequate. Intravitreal steroids carry a high risk of ocular hypertension.

sections.title: Critical Warnings
content: ANTICOAGULANTS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED.
Ciclosporine should be avoided in patients with CNS involvement (neurotoxicity risk).
Infliximab requires TB screening (risk of reactivation).
Visual loss rate in women is roughly half that in men.
Arterioles are affected later than veins in the retina.
